624282,ca.proc.d.1922-04-20.1.10.8,1922-04-20,81e9d110-f6b1-4643-a4a5-d110dba9135f,ca.m.7827,Mr. MOTHERWELL:,Minister of Agriculture,QUESTIONS,PENITENTIARY ACT AMENDMENT,,It is a large

item. About half a million of the amount is to be expended in connection with the accredited herds. The object is to clean up tuberculosis especially in the pure bred herds and to compensate owners for animals slaughtered under this system. The method
Supply-Health of Animals

employed is thought to be practically the only way of, dealing with this matter. We may have been a little late in taking it up, but ""better late than never."" The amount asked for is the same as last year. I anticipate that we will be able to cover more ground with the present vote, by reason of the fact that cattle have gone down in price, and the chances are that before the session is over a bill will be brought down providing for a reduction in the amount of compensation in proportion to the present value of cattle. Consequently the present vote will cover a larger number of herds than the larger amount of compensation given for animals last year under the conditions which then existed.

How the system is administered; If operative in the nine provinces? How many herds were inspected last year, and what percentage of those inspected were found to be diseased?

,Progressive,,John Frederick Johnston,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=fac08547-64e9-47bf-a872-72ba942af77a&Language=E&Section=ALL
624286,ca.proc.d.1922-04-20.1.10.12,1922-04-20,81e9d110-f6b1-4643-a4a5-d110dba9135f,ca.m.7827,Mr. MOTHERWELL:,Minister of Agriculture,QUESTIONS,PENITENTIARY ACT AMENDMENT,,The system is in vogue in all the nine provinces of the Dominion. Naturally, in the older provinces that have been devoting their attention to dairying the greatest degree of tuberculosis is found and the system is taken advantage of to the greatest extent. I have not the exact figures as to the extent of the disease; the proportion varies. Some herds are found on inspection to be entirely tuberculous. When one-half or three-fourths of a herd are tuberculous it is practically the same as if the whole herd were affected, and you might as well clean up the entire lot. It is essentially a stable disease and the more animals you have in stables, especially where the stables are unsanitary, the more disease you have. Out on the prairies, where it has been the practice for the cattle to winter out, we have had very little of it. The disease operates quite like tuberculosis among human beings-it is a house disease among humans and a stable disease among cattle. Where the stables are ill-ventilated, even though the condition in other respects may be good, and the animals are kept under dairy conditions, you get a lot of tuberculosis; on the other hand if the cattle are out in the open air, as they were in the West up to lately, you do not have so much of it.

624289,ca.proc.d.1922-04-20.1.10.15,1922-04-20,a4a7d1fa-870b-4590-a260-7e2f460d6e83,ca.m.8566,Mr. TOLMIE:,,QUESTIONS,PENITENTIARY ACT AMENDMENT,,In that particular connection, very interesting experiments were carried on by Dr. Rutherford, when he was Veterinary Director General, in feeding tubercular and healthy animals together out of doors, and he found that where the animals were fed on the ground that they readily became infected, and that is one of the reasons why, on our ranches to-day, we find cattle affected with tuberculosis where this system of feeding is followed. The amount that used to be contributed for animals was $1,800. The old grant, up to a year or two years ago, was $1,800 plus $1,200, making $3,000. The institute compiles the crop statistics of the entire world at Rome, and disseminates the knowledge thus gained back to thirty-odd countries. The theory is that those engaged in agriculture will consult the statistics, and, if these show a world surplus of any kind of grain this year, they will be a little bit shy about sowing so much, and may sow less so as not to increase the glut. 624327,ca.proc.d.1922-04-20.1.10.53,1922-04-20,a4a7d1fa-870b-4590-a260-7e2f460d6e83,ca.m.8566,Mr. TOLMIE:,,QUESTIONS,PENITENTIARY ACT AMENDMENT,,"This appropriation for live stock is one of the most important that have appeared in the estimates of the Minister of Agriculture. I think it is generally admitted now that we cannot hope for a proper development of the agriculture of Canada until we reach a time when farmers generally adopt a system of mixed farming, with live stock playing a most important part. The history of the cultivation of this continent has shown us that, as the valleys were taken up and cultivated from time to time, where a one-crop system was followed, we had exhaustion of the soil resulting, and we found our settlers moving west from the Genesee valley in New York down into the corn belt, from there to the Pacific coast and then finally up into Canada. Let us compare this for a moment with results obtained in Great Britain where a system of mixed farming has been carried on for hundreds of years. Not only have the people of Great Britain produced and maintained in a high state of perfection more breeds of horses, cattle, sheep and swine, of high quality than all the rest of the world combined, but in Great Britain the yield of cereals per acre is greater than it is in Canada. That shows how important it is that we should get down to a system of mixed farming in this country at the earliest possible date.

A brief review of the live stock industry may be of interest on this occasion. We have in Canada about three and a half million horses, a great many of which are light horses. Although the automobile has driven a great many of them out of use, we find them, in many of the western provinces, quite a menace to the pastures, and as we cannot raise them at a profit we have to get rid of them. The enterprising Minister of Agriculture of Alberta even proposed to put them in pickle and send them over to the Belgians for food, but those people refused to have them, and we therefore have no market in that direction. There were some 26,000 head of these light horses in that province alone. The heavy horse is still much in demand, particularly on the farms of Canada, and there will be a good demand for this class of animal for many years to come. The market is getting barer every day, and it behooves breeders of heavy horses to see what can possibly be done to raise these heavy horses to a greater extent to meet the demands of the future.

As to cattle, we have about ten million head altogether, three and a half millions of which are dairy cows. It is an astonishing fact that at our abattoirs, where inspection is carried on and cattle are slaughtered for export and for home consumption, less than ten per cent of the animals slaughtered are good enough for export across the Atlantic. A great many of them are too small, too poor in quality, and altogether unsatsifactory in condition. The farmers thus suffer a tremendous loss by reason of the low standard of quality of the animals they ship to the market. Just the other day in the Toronto market, for example, the cheapest steer that was sold fetched 4i cents per pound, compared with 10 and 11 cents for the best, and, in one instance, 13 cents for an animal of first class condition. Farmers who send animals to market in poor condition lose heavily, first in the lower price they receive, and, secondly, in the lower weight of the animal as compared with stock in better condition. Farmers crowd animals on the market in the fall of the year, thus making conditions much worse than they would be if their shipments were spread over a longer period. Our 3,500,000 dairy cows last year produced wealth to the extent of some $260,000,000; and in this connection I might remark that I was very much interested the other day to hear, on the floor of the House, the statement that our dairymen could not hope to succeed unless they
Supply-Live Stock

worked their wives and families in the dairy. I do not think that this statement is applicable to the dairy districts of Ontario or British Columbia. I know that in British Columbia we are able to import our bran and shorts, the rough feeds, such as barley and oats, from the prairies, in many instances get our alfalfa from Washington, paying duty in addition to freight, and are able to make a profit, and, as well, have a hired man to help us. We cannot, however, hope to accomplish this with poor-quality cows. These 3,500,000 cows average only about 4,000 pounds of milk per cow per year. Now, we have certain animals in Canada that have made records of over 32,000 pounds per year, or eight times as much as the production of one of these average cows. This means that the man who wants to produce 32,000 pounds with scrub cows will require to maintain no fewer than eight of these animals, providing housing and feed, and giving them all the general attention necessary in a dairy. At the end of the year the man with the 32,000-pound cow will have made a substantial profit, while all that the other man gets with his scrub cattle in the way of profit is simply the fresh air and the exercise. This shows how necessary it is for us to improve the quality of our animals. And if there is any farmer in any part of Canada who requires more information along these particular lines, if he is anxious to improve his herd and feed it at a profit, all he has to do is to make inquiry of these much-criticised establishments, the Dominion experimental farms.

We have only about 3,725,000 sheep in Canada, which has a larger area than the United States. As against this comparatively small number of sheep in this country, Great Britain has some 27,000,000, the United States 40,000,000, and Australia between 80,000,000 and 90,000,000 sheep. It is true that wool is very low in price, and in view of conditions such as that, there is a general tendency to get out of the sheep business. On the other hand, mutton and lamb fetch a good price, and if the farmers had bought thin lambs last fall and fed them over the winter on much of the cheap food we hear them talking about, they would have been able to do this at a profit, besides obtaining a much larger figure per bushel for their grain.

We have about 4,500,000 hogs in Canada, which is a poor showing compared with the United States. Only last fall a feeder on the Pacific Coast wanted to purchase 6,000 head of hogs for feeding purposes, desiring the

supply extended over six or seven months, and he could not secure this number. It is interesting to know that while many of the farmers went out of the hog business because, as they claimed, hogs did not pay when grain was as high as it was during the period of the war and in the years immediately after, the hogs produced a profit every year at the Central Experimental Farm at Ottawa. If the farmers of Canada desire to know how this was done they can obtain this information also absolutely free of charge.

If there is one thing more than another that injures the farmers as a whole in this country, it is the in-and-out system of farming; that is to say, going in at the high price and tumbling out at the low price, and losing both ways. We must be consistent. We must adopt a system of mixed farming carried on consistently, and stand by it through the lean years as well as in the good years; and in the long run the farmer who does that will come out ahead of the game. It is also important that we should make a careful study of the market so that we may dispose of our goods to the best possible advantage. In connection with the Live Stock branch, we have a first class marketing organization that keeps in close touch with the markets throughout the country and also with the export markets, and the farmers can obtain the fullest information from this branch before disposing of their live stock. In my opinion, there are two great requisites for the live stock industry of this country: First, to obtain for our producers the best possible markets, on which they can rely at all times,-because the greatest inducement to the producer is the knowledge that when he has turned out a good article he can dispose of it at a satisfactory figure;-and second, we must improve the quality of our stock. As I have pointed out, there is great room for such an improvement in connection with not only our beef cattle, but also our dairy animals. We must also standardize our live stock product so that it can always go upon the market of the same high quality and in sufficient quantity to interest the buyer. Of the various export markets that we have, the* nearest and most convenient is the United States. I have no objection to shipping our goods to that market; in fact, I think we should support any reasonable measure that could improve that avenue to the Canadian farmer. A year ago last January, I had the pleasure of addressing the American National Live Stock Association at El Paso,
Supply-Live Stock

Texas. That association represented all the range cattle men of the states extending from Texas to California, north from California to Washington, and from Washington, east to the Dakotas. The range interests of the United States were, therefore, well represented. I attended the convention for three days and listened with interest to the discussions, and I came to the conclusion at that time that those men wanted protection. Apparently, from what is going on at Washington, they still want it; and I feel that we are going to be faced with the problem incident to that protection in the United States for some years to come. That, at least, was the opinion I formed after carefully studying the feeling of that convention. They discussed the whole situation and concluded that their export markets in Europe, being how in such a condition that they could not absorb the surplus of the United States, it was best for that country, for a few years at any rate, to consume at home as much of its products as possible. There was one thing that struck me as I listened to the discussions at that convention, and that was that while the American farmer, with the large markets at his door, is a protectionist, the farmer on this side is not so much interested in that question.

Another market that is offering to us is the British and it is a more suitable market, for the reason that there is less chance of any tinkering with the tariff. At the present time, as hon. members are perhaps aware, we can dispose of our live animals at Birkenhead and Glasgow on condition that they are slaughtered within ten days of arrival. This, of course, is not a very advantageous way to sell our live stock. As can be readily understood, with the shrewd British dealer at the other end, and the owner of the cattle three thousand miles from home, with only ten days in which to sell them, the advantage is decidedly on the side of the dealer in England. But the embargo has not yet been removed and we have therefore to sell under those conditions. However, this market is useful at the present time. It may be asked: Why does it not pay us to kill our cattle on this side and send them ovter as chilled beef? The answer is: Simply because we cannot face the competition of the Argentine. She 'is able to put chilled beef on the British market at a very much lower price than we can and of as high quality, and the Britisher will pay a great deal more for fresh-killed beef than for chilled beef. So it pays us
to ship our cattle on the hoof rather than as chilled or frozen beef.

That 'brings me to the point: Why do we want the British embargo against our cattle withdrawn? For the reason that in Canada we do not possess either the facilities or sufficient trained men for the finishing of our cattle so that we can ship them to the British market in a fat or finished condition. In 1919 We sent 500,000 cattle to the United States to be fattened. These feeders were taken over by the Americans and put in shape in Pennsylvania and in the corn states and then sent to the British market. In 1920 we sent 312,000 feeders to the States for the same purpose. Until we can get our men trained and install the necessary equipment to feed the stock at home, it will be necessary to look focr a market for such stock.

I am very glad to hear from the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) that he has been impressing on the British Government the desirability of lifting the cattle embargo. Perhaps a brief history of this embargo would be interesting. It has been in operation now for about thirty years, having been first imposed on the assumption that in a shipment of cattle from Canada to Great Britain one animal was found affected with contagious pleuropneumonia. That disease had never been known to exist in this country, and it did not exist at the time, nor has it ever existed here since. This animal was traced to the farm from which the shipment originated, and all the other cattle there werte found to be absolutely free from the disease and in a general healthy condition. It is now acknowledged that the diagnosis made at that time by the British veterinarians was erroneous. However, the embargo has 'been maintained for all these years.

I might give a brief resume of the efforts made to have the embargo removed. I think the honours are about even, inasmuch as every Canadian government, and every federal Minister of Agriculture since the embargo was put on thirty years ago has made all possible efforts to have it lifted. These efforts were abated during the war, but were renewed with increased vigour immediately after the armistice. The withdrawal of the embargo was strongly urged by Sir Robert Borden, .who in 1917 was successful in obtaining a promise from the then British Minister of Agriculture to the effect that the embargo would be lifted. About that time or shortly after Professor Roberston, representing the De-
Supply-Live Stock

partment of Agriculture, and Mr. Arkell, the present Live Stock Commissioner, also carried on, with the consent of the British authorities, very valuable work in Great Britain along the same lines. A brisk campaign was carried on during 1919, 1920 and 1921. While no advertising was done, and while no attempt was made to make political capital out of what was done by the federal Department of Agriculture, I am quite sure the right hon. leader of *the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) will back me up when I say that a continuous campaign was carried on during those years with the British authorities for the purpose of having the embargo removed. In 1921 the British commission appointed to deal with the matter gave its decision in favour of Canada. This was a very important step towards the lifting of the embargo. In addition to this a great deal of very valuable work has been accomplished by various associations in Great Britain. Allow me to mention a few of these organizations: The National Farmers' Union of Scotland; the Central Highland Association of Scotland; the Free Importation of Canadian Cattle Association of Great Britain; the Scottish Federal Meat Traders Association; the Live Stock Traders' Association of Great Britain; the Journeyman Butchers' Federation of Great Britain; the Union of London Meat Traders, whose President, Mr. Edwards, has carried on a very vigorous campaign for many years for the lifting of the embargo. Mr. Henderson, of Coupav Angus, Scotland, also has done very valuable work along the same lines. So it is quite clear that efforts to remove the embargo have been practically continuous on both sides of the Atlantic.

It is rather interesting, then, under these conditions to hear on the floor of this House and to note in a certain section of the agricultural press, that to Hon. Manning Doherty, Minister of Agriculture for Ontario, is due most of the credit for what has been accomplished. One enthusiastic paper in fact crowned him ""The Embargo King."" It is very doubtful indeed if the results obtained by Mr. Doherty were not overshadowed by the resentment created in Great Britain by his action there. His campaign was looked on as an uncalled-for interference on the part of a provincial minister in what was strictly federal work, and that he acted without any authority or any standing whatever in dealing with what was a strictly federal matter. In fact, the situation became so acute that the
[Mr. Tolmie.l

British Minister of Agriculture at that time issued a statement to the effect that when he got ready to deal with the embargo question he would do so through the proper channel-the federal government-and not through any provincial minister.

Canadians who have become domiciled there, but it is an entirely different matter for a Canadian who has no standing to attempt to dictate internal politics in that country.""

Without doubting Mr. Doherty's sincerity at all, from what I saw and heard in Great Britain I am of the opinion that so far as the British Government is concerned our case would have been in a much better position had Mr. Doherty refrained from interfering in federal affairs.

It was shortly after the coronation of Mr. Doherty that Mr. Drury, no doubt feeling somewhat envious over his colleague's ascension to the embargo throne, issued a statement at a meeting in Ontario to the effect that the British embargo would be lifted even if he had to go over there himself. I am quite sure he must have been joking. "" It's not done,"" as the Englishman would say, for any one to go over to England and try and compel these men on their own ground to do what they do not want to do. It has become a little out of fashion. The last man that made a success of it, I think, was William the Conqueror in 1066. One has only to see men like the Right Hon. Lloyd George, Right Hon. Winston Churchill, Lord Birkenhead, and a few more of those big guns in action, and then merely to think of Mr. Drury, to really enjoy the humour of the thing.

I think with the minister that there is a good chance of having the embargo removed, but we cannot hope to gain any success in this direction by any such methods as have been followed by any of the gentlemen I have mentioned. We cannot hope to accomplish anything by the creation of "" embargo kings."" We cannot hope to get anywhere by extravagant articles in the press nor by any cheap bluster. We must meet these men and negotiate with them in an orderly, decent, businesslike way, and I am quite sure that if we do they will give us a good hearing and be glad to deal with us. But if we do not do that, if we adopt the other method I have just outlined, all we can expect is that we shall make a laughingstock of this country and not get anywhere.

There was another criticism launched against the late government in some of the agricultural press to the effect that we were not properly represented at the embargo commission. We were criticised particularly because we did not have a legal representative there. You can quite understand that it was no part of the business of the commission to lift the embargo. That could only be done by an amendment to the Animal Diseases Act of Great Britain. The commission sat for the purpose of taking evidence and coming to a decision. We won one hundred per cent on that decision; we got everything we expected; so I do not see how a more favourable verdict could have been reached. Again, in ordinary business life there are two classes of people I have always carefully sidestepped: the lawyers, and plumbers. I can see no reason why we should have had legal representation before the commission, because we had no legal fight with the government of Great Britain. They were simply giving us an opportunity of presenting our case clearly before them; that we did, and as I say, we got a very satisfactory verdict. So we did not lose anything by not having a legal representative.

While the embargo in Great Britain is imposed on cattle coming from all countries, the excuse has been made by some Britishers that if they permitted cattle to come in from Canada, that would necessarily mean that all other countries would have the same privilege. But it was clearly pointed out to them in the
column4: Canadian case that this need not be so. In fact, it was clearly proven before the commission that Canadian herds were freer from contagious disease than any other herds in the world. Therefore, it would be a very easy matter indeed to pass regulations on a disease-free basis, so that by naming the various diseases Canadian cattle could easily be permitted to enter Great Britain without allowing cattle from other countries to get into that market.

column1: It might be interesting just to give a few of the points in connection with the arguments used by the British people. In the first place, Canadian stores can be shipped to the United States, France, Belgium, Switzerland and Germany, but we are not allowed the same privilege as regards Great Britain. Since the embargo was imposed thirty years ago, no less than 3,000,000 head of cattle have been landed on British shores from Canada, have been slaughtered under careful inspection, and not one single case of contagious pleuro-pneumonia or foot-and-mouth disease has been found. Why should we not have the same privilege as Ireland? Ireland is clamouring to be given the same dominion status as Canada, but still she objects to the entrance of Canadian cattle to Great Britain. The fact is that in Ireland they had foot-and-mouth
Supply-Live Stock

disease only a few months ago; they may have some now, whereas the only occasions when Canada had the disease on her shores was in 1884, when a ship called the Mississippi landed at Point Levis quarantine station in the month of May with cattle. Another ship, the Oxenholme, landed there a few months later. Both of these consignments were stopped there and dealt with at the quarantine station, and foot-and-mouth disease never gained a foothold in Canada. Strangely enough, both these shipments came from Great Britain.

The argument has been made that there is a possibility of disease coming in from the United States. That was met by this argument. In Canada, along a boundary of about 4,000 miles, about 1,700 of which is water, we have quarantine stations situated at various points, presided over by fully qualified representatives of the Health of Animals branch who make a careful inspection of all animals coming from the south, and even though they have had three outbreaks of foot-and-mouth disease in the United States, the last in the year 1914, when their losses amounted to millions of dollars, not one single case was permitted to cross the line and gain a foothold in Canada. So that the fact that we have been able successfully to protect our boundary line against disease from the United States for many years past, and are doing it today, is a sufficient guarantee of what we can do in the future.

Another point brought up was that once we get access to the British market, the United States might ship their cattle to Canada, and then across to the British market as Canadian cattle. That argument was met by this: it would be quite easy for the Department of Agriculture to brand permanently every animal coming in from the United States, except pedigree animals -which are readily enough recognized, and in any case would not be shipped as stores -and so make it utterly impossible for United States cattle to.be shipped across to the British market as ours. The next argument was that there was a great danger of Canadians glutting the British market and lowering the prices. Now the Canadian would be the last one to want that to happen, because he is under heavy expense in sending his animals over there. In fact at the present time if a 1,200 pound steer is picked up in Calgary and shipped to the British market the sum of $55 would have to be paid in freight alone which should be at least a sufficient handicap to export and sufficient protection for the

producers of store cattle in Great Britain. Now we admit that the Britisher has every right to protect his own market, but it is well to bear these two or three points in mind. In the first place we have had a distinct promise to the Prime Minister of this country that the embargo would be lifted. That promise has not been fulfilled. We have had a favourable finding by the Embargo Commission appointed by the British Government to inquire fully into this whole embargo question, and in the finding of that commission they not only declared that Canadian cattle were very free from contagious disease but that there was no danger to British herds from contagious disease from this country.

There is one other point I would like to draw to the attention of the minister, and that is that, while it has been clearly shown that there is no danger to British herds from disease from cattle coming from Canada, our cattle are still kept out of Great Britain by the Animals Diseases Act, an act maintained for the purpose of protecting British herds from disease. Before leaving the subject of embargo I would like to take this opportunity to thank the British Embargo Commission, headed by Lord Finlay, for the courtesy extended to the Canadian representatives. They gave us every opportunity to present our case as fully as possible and treated us with the utmost fairness. I also wish to take this opportunity to thank Sir George Perley, the Canadian High Commissioner at that time, and his assistant Mr. Griffiths, for many services rendered. Sir Howard d'Eggville, Secretary of the Empire Parliamentary Association, was another gentleman who did everything possible to make our trip to England very pleasant and gave us every assistance and all the information we required in presenting our case. Hon. Duncan Marshall, who was then Minister of. Agriculture for Alberta; presented very valuable and practical information before the commission. Lord Beaverbrook, a Canadian who owns a string of newspapers over there and who has persistently fought for the lifting of the embargo has rendered Canada good service along this line.

While I was in Britain I took advantage of the opportunity to study the situation in the British market for Canadian live stock products. I found that we are faced with brisk competition in that market, the competition coming from Denmark, Sweden, Holland, the United States, Argentina and New Zealand. If we are to obtain a strong foothold and be able to com-

pete with these other countries our goods must be high and uniform in quality and of sufficient volume to interest those men on the other side. The European shipping his bacon to the British market has a decided advantage over us to a
he is able to put his goods on the market so much sooner than we can. He can put his bacon there with a lighter cure and this is preferred by the British consumer. I found the British traders

shrewd people; they are anxious to patronize the British dominions just as long as those dominions can furnish them with goods of high quality and just as cheaply as they can get them from other countries, and they cannot be blamed for this.

While over there I was very pleased to note that there was a strong move to increase trade within the Empire, and that in 1923 an exhibition will be held in London at which an opportunity will be given to all the dominions to exhibit their products and their manufactures, and I sincerely hope that the Government will take advantage of this opportunity to make a good strong exhibit of Canadian products. With reference to the other markets offering, I may say that on the Pacific coast there has 'been a start, even though in a small way, in the shipping of pure bred cattle to Australia, New Zealand, the Hawaiian Islands, China and Japan. This does not give promise of any immediate development, but it nevertheless offers possibilities for the future. With regard to the proposal to Send representatives to South America, mentioned by the Minister of Agriculture a day or two ago, I think it is a good move. The representation of the beef men should, however, be spread among the breeds. Not only should the Shorthorn men he represented but also the Hereford and Polled Angus breeders. Mr. L. O. Clifford, of Oshawa, is one of the best breeders of Hereford cattle in the country. Mr. J. D. McGregor, of Brandon, is one of the largest breeders of Polled Angus in the world. On several occasions he has gone to the exhibitions in the United States and carried off prizes. Either of these men would make a very good representative. In addition, the dairy interest
should be represented as I pointed out a day or two ago.

A far better plan to promote the development of the live stock industry-and I am fully aware of the difficulties in the way having had a little experience in the Department of Agriculture-would be to use all our pure bred stock at home. As I have pointed out, the quality of our beef cattle on the whole is poor, and the same thing may be said of our dairy cattle. While there are some excellent specimens, and while, perhaps, our cattle are as good as the average in other countries, still there is a great deal of room for improvement; I think everything possible should be done to have nearly all the pure bred stock retained in this country because there is an excellent field here for development.

One other point before I close, and that is with regard to the matter of grants for exhibitions referred to a day or two ago. I think it is very inopportune to cut this grant at the present time, particularly for the smaller shows that qualify under the present regulations of the Government, or as they existed a year ago. There were poor crops last year, and the exhibitions will be on before our farmers have had an opportunity to realize on the crops of 1922. The result is there is a general tightness of money in the country and the receipts of these exhibitions will not be as good as usual. I have already pointed out that [DOT]notwithstanding what they have done in connection with the live stock business there is room for a great deal more development along this line, and the expenditure of $180,000, such as the minister mentioned the other day, to assist the cattle shows which have a value of from one and a half to two billion dollars is not a very large sum. I understand, too, that these men have not received notification of the change determined upon and consequently they will suffer great hardship in meeting the situation this year when the markets are flat and prices are low and the demands are not very good for pure bred stock. Therefore every possible effort should be made to interest people in exhibiting their live stock, particularly at the present time. Why? Because there never is a time when it is so desirable that there should be good stock as when prices are low. When that is the case there is always the possibility of making a little money out of a good animal but no prospect at all of making any out of a scrub.

624330,ca.proc.d.1922-04-20.1.10.56,1922-04-20,81e9d110-f6b1-4643-a4a5-d110dba9135f,ca.m.7827,Mr. MOTHERWELL:,Minister of Agriculture,QUESTIONS,PENITENTIARY ACT AMENDMENT,,I thank my hon. friend from Victoria City (Mr. Tolmie) for his very concise and comprehensive resume of the live stock situation in Canada, more particularly for his remarks concerning the cattle embargo, with the exception of his strictures with respect to the Hon. Manning Doherty. I was on the farm busy trying to make both ends meet at the time the incident occurred to which he has alluded, and therefore I am not familiar with the facts and cannot say whether his remarks are justified to the fullest extent or not. I can say this, however, that all my relations with Mr. Doherty since I came down here have been both satisfactory and pleasant. So much for that.

The rest of my hon. friend's remarks were excellent and I want to thank him for thsm. We do not have sufficient speeches of that character. We have not yet realized in the West, and perhaps in other parts of Canada, that, after all, the corner-stone of agriculture in Canada, as elsewhere, is the live stock industry. We are gradually getting to it, not by choice always, but sometimes by compulsion, by the stern necessities of the case, by the climatic conditions and the soil conditions, lack of fertility and otherwise; and a speech such as my hon. friend delivered accelerates the action in that direction. I will not try to improve on it at all, for fear I should spoil it. I will simply try to accentuate one or two points. First, there is the necessity of paying more attention to quality in our live stock, both beef and dairying. Let any man take a trip to any of our abattoirs-the one, particularly that I am familiar with, in Winnipeg-and he will see a lot of fine stock there. But the rubbish which will be found there is distressing, especially in a dry year. They will hardly pay for their haulage to Winnipeg, especially during the recent years. As a matter of fact, I do not think some of them do pay for haulage. But if we can keep such good stock as some of these animals are, get along at all, and not go into debt, then it should pay to keep them.

As regards the dairy interests, the keeping of more and better live stock in some of our prairie provinces is very important, and upon that depends the future of southern Alberta and southwest Saskatchewan. There is no question about that. We must go into live stock, dairying, associated with siloing and the con-

struction of silos. The drought there makes necessary the feeding of cattle in summer and winter, and the only way I know of by which they can obtain the necessary provender is to have an abundance of silage, not only during the winter but also till the middle of summer. That is not a new view in regard to live stock. Forty or fifty years ago, as a youth, I cut corn with a sickle, and fed the animals after school in the dry times, all summer, in order to keep up the flow of milk. If you go round Ontario, you will hardly find any feeding, except in the silo. They have a drought all over Canada, but not for so many consecutive years as in the prairies, and I am just as satisfied as I can be of anything that with due attention to the proper quality of beef and dairy live stock we can succeed. On those portions of the prairie we hear a great deal about the great drought, and it is terrible; unless you experience it you know nothing of it. But the cultivation of fodder-corn, sunflowers, sweet clover and all such plants

accompanied by the construction of silos, will be the salvation of agriculture in that important and unfortunate part of our western prairies. They are just on the balance now. A touch, or almost a breath, would send them the wrong way, but a little nursing will bring them back and put them on the highway to a reasonable development and to prosperity. I am satisfied these remarks will apply to many parts of Canada besides the particular area I have in my mind, and I am thankful to my hon. friend for stressing this feature of agriculture as he has done, if it is only for that particular aspect of the agricultural situation.

My hon. friend referred very briefly to the necessity of markets. There is no use lamenting the loss of the American market. We lost our chance, Mr. Chairman, and I do not know whether we will get it again or not. Every man who has an animal to sell, every hour of the day and every day of the week, thinks of what might have been. I do not want to be pessimistic, but the worse it looks in that direction-and I think it looks pretty bad [DOT]-the more necessity of looking to the British market and the removal of the embargo. There are other markets, but they are only minor compared with those two great markets. It may be that our American friends will come to themselves later on, as we have come to ourselves, and that some time we may meet when we will
Supply-Live Stock
both see alike, and may consummate a bargain of a sensible nature. But to-day we might as well realize the position and look elsewhere for the markets of the immediate future.

My hon. friend's references to the in-and-out system of agriculture, especially with regard to hog growing, is apt and timely. We have been going in and out ever since I can remember, but our friends the Progressives will tell you there are other reasons why they went in and out. I am not going to refer to that very much. I think, possibly, if we remained a little bit more steadfast, as my hon. friend suggested, and took the shadow with the sunshine, we would hit it sometime. Jumping in and out continuously, you may miss it every time, but if you stay with it you will hit it sometime or other. I do not want to go into the question of why this is so. We have been doing it for fifty years, and the average man will tell you he is justified in doing so. Sometimes we go out of a thing simply because of anger. We get so provoked when we have something to sell, and cannot sell it, that we throw it to one side and say ""I'm not going to bother with it."" I do not think that is a wise course, but it is the natural one.

With reference to the embargo question, we have listened to a very interesting and, I think, very thorough, recital. I will not dwell upon the matter now but will only say that I intimated, when we were discussing this matter the latter part of last month, that as soon as the new High Commissioner arrived in London I wrote him on the subject of this embargo. Before he left I had a long conversation with him. He is very much interested in it himself. He does want to be useful to Canada, and he sees no way he could be more useful immediately than by assisting in the removal of this handicap. I immediately wrote him, therefore, suggesting certain measures to secure the entry of our cattle into London, or to the outskirts of London, as that would make an immense market, and, I have instructed the representative of the Agricultural Department to call upon Mr. Larkin as soon as he arrives in England, and discuss the matter with him in the light of the present day events. I have asked him to seek an interview with Right Hon. Winston Churchill, because he is the gentleman who is at present in the limelight on this important question. I observe that he is making speeches indicating the likelihood of some changes on the part of the Gov-

ernment there. They expect to have an open, free-for-all vote on 3rd May on the question. Knowing something of governments, it seems to me they are simply preparing for a change and they are going to throw the responsibility on Parliament to make the change, and I am in hopes Parliament will act wisely with regard to this particular question primarily, and incidentally also with respect to ourselves. In addition to that, I think I would be justified in telling the committee-although I cannot give them anything very definite at this time-that this Government is in cable communication with the highest officials in Great Britain, 'and has been for the last week, with respect to this important matter. Later on in the session we may be able to place those cablegrams before this House, but it is not in the interest of the movement itself to say very much about it at this particular time.

Now we come to the question of grants to exhibitions. Here we have an illustration of how hard it is for a government to reduce expenditure. We all have to try that out sooner or later. If you go to dismiss some unfortunate civil servant that you think you can dispense with, who is not much good, before nightfall every friend at Ottawa is clamouring on his behalf. Now what are you going to do if you have a heart at all?

624332,ca.proc.d.1922-04-20.1.10.58,1922-04-20,81e9d110-f6b1-4643-a4a5-d110dba9135f,ca.m.7827,Mr. MOTHERWELL:,Minister of Agriculture,QUESTIONS,PENITENTIARY ACT AMENDMENT,,I certainly have great sympathy with the representatives of this city in this House. Things are bad enough for the rest of us, but I do not know how they exist to-day.

With respect to these grants, I think I made it quite plain before, on the civil government estimates, that we had in mind cutting these grants in two, on the assumption that the various exhibition authorities had been notified. It was my impression that they had been notified; but I find that they have not been, and it would be rather drastic, without proper warning, to cut those grants in two all at once. I think, however, a very good principle to adopt would be that adopted by the late government with respect to reducing the bonus to civil servants by 25 per cent. I do not know whether, if they had had the opportunity, they intended to continue cutting down the bonus until it all disappeared, or how they proposed to deal with it, but they started all right; instead of

taking a hatchet and smashing the bonus all to pieces at one blow, they tempered the wind to the shorn lamb by reducing the bonus gradually. In the first place, I take 'the ground that the question of grants to agricultural societies is strictly a provincial matter. There may be a few exceptions, winter fairs or something of that nature as regards which I would not care to express an opinion offhand; but, generally speaking, I think this should be a provincial and local matter. I am not going to criticise my predecessor. I think it was Hon. Mr. Burrell who introduced these federal grants with, no doubt, the best of intentions; but that was a day of spending large sums of money; that was a day when small contributions from individuals were hard to get, and there was some justification for his putting his hand into the public treasury and being liberal to these exhibitions which found it hard to finance during the early days of the war, and later. That, however, is no justification to-day for continuing these grants. Some of the exhibitions have now substantial surpluses as a result of these grants. I know a city in Saskatchewan-I will not mention the name; it is not the one that I represent anyway-that receives from this Parliament a grant of $5,000, and, in addition to that, receives $11,000 from the provincial government. Now that we are getting these gilt-edged highways and high-powered cars, people come scurrying into these centres from a hundred miles around and if exhibition day is fine, the authorities take in all kinds of money. They pay their secretaries high salaries and put everybody else in the air who does not get the same amount for his services. Farmers -complain, with some ground, that salaries paid in the cities make it difficult for them to compete in the labour market. That is exactly what we are doing ourselves with respect to these exhibition grants, making 'it difficult for other people to get help when these high salaries are being paid. If we bad oceans of money, it might be all right to shovel it out, but we have to cut down expenditure as much as possible. 1 see my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) smiling. He knows as well as I do how difficult it is to rub along. Things may improve, but in the meantime, we must keep close watch on all expenditures. My good friends, the Progressives, sometimes want to know what is the necessity of all this expenditure on statistics and what not, and yet they will come blithely at me and ask me to continue these grants. Well, that is about all they

can do, and I presume it is what I would do myself; but this simply means that I have not to take them too seriously when they want this, that or the other item cut down, because you cannot have the money and spend it at the same time. After discussing the matter with my deputy and others, I think that possibly, instead of cutting these grants in half, we shall be able to do with a 25 per cent reduction. The exhibition managers will receive 75 per cent of the grant that has been in vogue in the past, and they should be able to get along lacking the 25 per cent. That is what the Civil Service had to do last year, and I do not know yet what they will have to do this year. That is the principle that has been laid down and it seems to be a rational one. Perhaps, next year, the grant can be cut down another 25 per cent, and the last two cuts will, perhaps, come more easily. I am not criticising the introduction of these grants because I was not here then, and it may have been all right; but, at present, when the sources of revenue for exhibitions are more than they were and revenues much more buoyant, when roads are in better shape, when many more people have cars, and when, if exhibition day happens to be a good one, there is no trouble in financing the affair, this sum of $180,000 could be expended on something else that would be (productive of better results. In the meantime, what I have stated will likely be our policy, unless this Parliament says that these grants must be continued as before and it votes the money. That, however, will not be on my advice.

It does enter into competition with milk, but it is milk with the butter fat content mostly taken from it and then evaporated. In fact, it is cleaner and more sanitary than real milk, because, as a rule, greater precaution is taken in the manufacture of it than in the actual putting of whole milk on the market, especially in the winter time. doing here. The stockmen located along the Water ton river too, seven miles below the Waterton lake, lost 35 head last year. I lost 5 head, 4 head of yearlings in four days. The range along the foothills that the cattle run on is all partly covered by scrub timber and brush, and, the number of cattle stated in these letters-
That is, those that were killed, I take it.
-were all seen by the owners, so only partly represent the total loss; yet the number is over one hundred for one year from a few men.
One of the letters he encloses is signed by Sam and John Walburger. It reads:

We have been asked to state the number of calves lost, and yearlings, in the Dominion park, east of the Belly river. Yearlings, 21 per cent, 7 per cent of sucking calves, during the summer of 1921. And would like to state that the sucking calves got away very light.
There is another letter signed by J. J. West, who states his loss as follows:
Colts year 1921, 3 head, under 1 year.
Cattle year 1921, 11 head, from calves to two year olds.
Cdlts year 1922, 5 head, under 1 year.
*Cattle year 1922, 7 head, from calves to two year olds.

Another man last year lost 14 head, from yearlings up, and 10 head of calves. I will not go into all these letters, because the time is short. I want to impress upon the members of this House, however, and especially upon the minister, that it is quite as important to protect our live stock from the dangers to which they are exposed from wild animals, as it is to take measures to prevent tuberculosis and other diseases. The minister did me the kindness to mention the fact that I had called to his attention the tuberculosis situation in the Lethbridge district. I was very much interested in that matter. I am also greatly interested in the present subject I am discussing, and I will ask the minister to see that provision is made in some way for an adequate bounty to put a stop to the loss which the stockmen in this district experience from wolves. They made an effort themselves, and I see by one of the letters that they donated quite a sum of money for the purpose. But I imagine that their efforts were of no effect, one reason being that the breeding grounds of the wolves are on Dominion property, and I do not think that the stockmen are allowed to go on these reserves with their guns. One of the letters says:

The stockmen in this district four years ago met and offered a bounty of $60 for each female and $40 for males and $20 for pups. Since that time we have only been called on to pay bounty on seven pups, one female and one male.

So that they do not seem to make any progress through their voluntary efforts, and some arrangement should be made to rid these public reserves and parks of the wolves that are coming out and preying on herds of stock. We are trying to develop a good stock and dairy country in that part of the Dominion. In this immediate neighbourhood, which comes within the district of my hon. friend from Macleod (Mr. Coote), they are developing an irrigation project covering some 23,000 acres, one of the main purposes of which is the encouragement of dairy and stock raising. I take the ground that these people should not be subjected to losses incurred by reason of wild animals preying on their stock. I hope the minister will take this matter under advisement and make such provision as will protect farmers and stock-raisers against these losses. To enable him to deal with the matter I intend to turn these communications over to him.

Possibly he has not and on the other hand he may. The matter is worth looking * into. Packers in this country are not any more likely to be the super-packers than are Canadian hog producers likely to be superior to the Danish-hog producer. An hon. member stated this afternoon something about the amount of money there is in hogs. One of my constituents gave me his experience when a similar statement was made to him. He said, ""Certainly, I believe there is money in hogs. There is a bunch of hogs:

in them than I can ever get out. So I am Quite satisfied there is money in hogs."" I hope the hon. Minister of Agriculture will give some thought to the question of the curing as well as the production of bacon, because the farmer cannot cure the bacon; that is the work of the packer; and I think that maybe the packer needs education in curing bacon as much as the farmer does in producing the bacon hog.

624359,ca.proc.d.1922-04-20.1.10.85,1922-04-20,6f0e79a6-263d-4f17-8fbc-6e37780ff83c,ca.m.8647,Mr. CALDWELL:,,QUESTIONS,PENITENTIARY ACT AMENDMENT,,While we are considering the live stock industry I would like to direct the minister's attention to a very great handicap upon the development of that industry in the maritime provinces. That is the lack of abattoir and cold storage facilities for that section of Canada due to the fact that our live stock, even that which is raised for home consumption in the maritime provinces, must be
Supply-Live Stock

shipped to Montreal to take advantage of the abattoir and cold storage facilities there, from which city the product is shipped back again to the consumers in the maritime provinces. I think, Mr. Chairman, you will realize that with the present very high freight rates such a condition results in too wide a spread between the producer and the consumer, a spread you cannot get away from under present conditions. 624361,ca.proc.d.1922-04-20.1.10.87,1922-04-20,b518c3e0-9d1a-43c2-8a1e-a14029b83b97,ca.m.4509,Mr. STANSELL:,,QUESTIONS,PENITENTIARY ACT AMENDMENT,,I would like some information on one or two points from the minister or his deputy. However, I have inquired, and received the information, through Hansard, that there is no such appointment now, but, in spite of that fact, there is an increase of $10,000 here, making a total increase of $127,360. but when we come to the diseases of animals, and everything that can possibly be done under this head for the improvement and betterment of the live stock industry as well as the health of the animals there is no increase. I am only going to point out two particulars that occur to me. Under this vote I understand we have the administration of what is known as the ""Canadian Record of Performance."" This was established some 17 or 18 years ago in a small way, I believe, under the Laurier regime, and in the opinion, I presume, of many hon. members of this House, that would be a sufficient guarantee of its high standard of perfection. This work is something that naturally grows from year to year and it is a work I have intimate knowledge of. I have been told by many who are taking advantage of the work of this department, and by many on the staff, that the work is not being properly done at present for lack of sufficient inspectors and the lack of staff is attributed to the lack of money. So much has this work been appreciated by the stock breeders that, since Parliament has been in session, a delegation representing various live stock associations met with the Live Stock Commissioner to talk over this question, and, though you may be surprised to hear it, so much did they appreciate this work that, although the money has been granted, and the expenditure has been carried on by the department, these men have given a cash grant of somewhere between five and ten thousand dollars, in order that this work may be carried on. be properly met without increasing the amount?

Then there is the subject of the accredited herd, which comes either under this or the health of animals vote in which also there is no increase over the vote of the previous year. Canada, has within the scope of its financial ability, done more for agriculture than has the Government of Nova Scotia. I also understand that the Dominion government is going to lend sires of pure breeds for dairying purposes, etc. At the same time, the difficulty that we see in the way is this. In every small community we have about five or six farmers who are engaged in mixed farming, and they are the ones who are making good; but, because of low prices of grain last year, many others went into mixed farming, saving all the cream that they could possibly save in order to get a little money, with the result that, instead of their getting the amount of money they expected for cream, butter and eggs, they got about fifteen to twenty cents per pound for butter and about the same per dozen for eggs. The question that we are concerned with is this. If all the people of southern Saskatchewan enter into mixed farming, as has been advocated by many agriculturists as the salvation of our western country, where are we going to find markets? Has the minister any scheme or has he thought of any outlet whereby we can get rid of our surplus stock over local needs? That is the pressing question for us at the present

time; and as I look over this estimate, I am not able to see where he has made any arrangement for getting larger markets for the product that will naturally result from people entering into this mixed farming which he advocates. Whenever a department takes up any new work the officials are loath to see it disorganized, and you have that spirit to contend with. There is a great difficulty in disestablishing things and starting over again, and the process always takes time. My two predecessors were not sufficiently long on the job to make any great change, and I was going to express the hope that I might hold office long enough to give some effect to the good intentions we have in this matter. However, I will not dwell on that suggestion. If I am so honoured I hope to be able to meet the hon. gentleman's representations and endeavour to abolish the overlapping as far as it is possible to do so. It did seem to be a badly organized affair. However, after
some delay and confusion we were able to start these gentlemen off west rejoicing.

The member for Battleford (Mr. Mc-Conica), in his own amusing style, referred to the difficulty involved in the wool business. I do not know whether the hon. gentleman is present or not, but I may be able to explain the question of sending the sheep after the wool to pay the deficit. Some members of the committee know that the British government, before the war was over, secured a large quantity of wool in anticipation of a protracted state of warfare. Among other countries, they bought wool very largely from Australia for several years, and they have been taking the wool off Australia's hands at the high price engaged for during the war, and: feeding the market with it as slowly a& possible, having regard to the fact that they had to get rid of it at some time. Nevertheless, in spite of the slowness with which they fed the market, they glutted it, with the result that wool is now a drug on the market. The large stocks accumulated in England in anticipation of a long drawn out war had to go on the market, and this created a congested condition from which we have not yet recovered. I may refer to a similar condition in regard to another industry, and it will be a solace to those who are going into mixed farming to find that there is a valid explanation for the extraordinary state of things with regard to butter. Great Britain's stocks of butter were so generous at the close of the war that she finally got rid of them only last July. They were procured at high prices and sold at low prices, and the last consignment went to Belgium, consisting of 1,000,000 boxes of 56 pounds each, or 56,000,000 pounds of butter for which Belgium has twenty years to pay. It is therefore obvious how long it has taken to adjust affairs after the great upheaval due to the war. Now that these stocks have been got rid of, new production will have a better chance of being disposed of in the future than during the last year or two. I am sure that these explanations will be accepted. They are facts, and they indicate, I think, a hopeful prospect, as well as the circumstances that we have reached the bottom in the matter of bad prices. This knowledge, of course, does not put any more money into your pocket just now; but if there is a bad condition of affairs and you can explain it and show that it is not likely to recur, it does hold out some hope for the future.

The member for Victoria and Carle ton (Mr. Caldwell) brought up the subject of cold storage in the maritime provinces. I was rather surprised myself to find, when making inquiry into a certain condition of affairs in connection with the live stock industry, that there was only one cold storage abattoir in the three maritime provinces, located at Charlottetown. There is a reason f.or that, but the fact remains that they have only one and want more. Now, apart from any provincial effort which those provinces may make, the only hope I can hold out to my hon. friends is that, in the not too distant future, we may be able to amend the present Cold Storage Act in such a way as to carry out the original intention of helping other cooperative plants than municipal plants, which are the only ones that are aided at the present time. Formerly the act applied to any .cold storage plants put up either by individuals or by co-operative companies. Under the provisions of that act, any cold storage company, complying with the regulations, received from the federal government 30 per cent of the cost of erection as an encouragement in the establishing of such plants. About three or four years ago the act was changed to apply only to municipal plants, and scarcely a dollar has been spent since that amendment. When we have a little more money in the treasury upon which we can draw, we hope to revert to the original condition and permit the maritime provinces to avail themselves of the substantial subsidy which is allowed for erecting cold storage plants. In Saskatchewan a number of plants were erected under this system before the change, and it was a great stimulus to this enterprise. Just now, however the treasury would not appear to be sufficiently buoyant to warrant the expenditures that would be entailed in this direction.

My hon. friend from Swift Current (Mr. Lewis) asks a very natural question: What shall we do with all these mixed farming products? Some of my recent remarks will apply the answer so far as wool is concerned. As regards butter and dairy products generally, and also beef cattle-and that is the direction in which I expect the greatest' development in southwest Saskatchewan in the future-I might inform my hon. friend that to-day we supply only 2J per cent of the total imports of butter of Great Britain. There is therefore abundant room for us in that market; we ought to be able to get some share of the other

97J per cent. True, there are a number of competitors like Denmark and little New Zealand. But it is for us, with improved methods and better cows, to meet that competition squarely and fairly. There is no doubt that while there is a limit to the market for milk, there is really none in sight in our time as regards butter, especially when we realize that we supply, as I have said, only 2J per cent of Great Britain's total importations of this commodity. With regard to other products, pork, bacon, eggs, etc., we have really never been stuck for a market. It is true that the supply of eggs fluctuates with the season, but with cold storage to take care of them in the spring and ease up the natural glut on the market at that time, it seems to me there would always be a fair market.

With regard to bacon, that is an article of world-wide production, and the surplus goes on to the British market where we have exactly the same competitors as in butter. If we produce a second or third grade article the problem of market will always be present; but if we provide a gilt-edged article in competition with Denmark and New Zealand, then we shall be able to secure the market. But we are not doing it now, for the reason that our bacon is not going on to the market graded, nor is proper attention being paid to the grading of hogs, with the result that we are struggling to retain what share of the British market we already have. We must improve our methods of production and the quality of our goods if we are to secure a greater share of that market.

I do not think my hon. friend from Swift Current (Mr. Lewis), was in the House this afternoon when the hon. member for Victoria City (Mr. Tolmie) and others were discussing the embargo question. There are very good hopes within a reasonable time of that embargo being removed. Of course, we are going to get it removed, and we are getting nearer to that end all the time. I cannot speak positively, but the situation is hopeful; and, after all, in this world we have more or less to live on hope.

It is true that when the depredations are due to wolves which are supposed to come from the forest reserves of the Dominion, damage claims may be made against my col-

league, the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart), who has charge of those reserves; but as far as I am aware no bounties have been given in the past by the Dominion government for the killing of these timber wolves. It is a matter that has always been dealt with by the provincial authorities, and there is no reason why those hunting timber wolves may not go on the timber reserves in search of these animals. I know that in Saskatchewan and Alberta the provincial governments have for many years paid bounties on wolves, I think twenty dollars on each adult animal, and so much less on pups. I think we are too far away from the scene of depredations to engage in a dual system of wolf bounties. If my hon. friends have had anything to do with the administration of the Wolf Bounty Act, they would know that it is a very difficult piece of work. I know that half a dozen timber wolves will do an enormous amount of damage against stock in a very short time, but that is purely a matter for the provincial authorities to handle, even although the wolves are on Dominion land.

The hon. member for East Elgin (Mr. Stansell) uttered what seemed to me to be very justifiable remarks about the smallness of some of the votes. I think most of us will agree that all of these votes are, if anything, too small. But last year, taking the Health of Animals branch there was an increase of some $300,000. Consequently that vote was put at a fairly high level, and it is not necessary to still further increase it this year. And, further, because of our intention to amend the act with respect to the valuation of the animals that are slaughtered, owing to the fact that the value of live stock has come down so substantially since the act was passed, to the extent of at least one-third, we are not justified in giving such a high valuation as obtained two years ago, and therefore we will be able with the same aggregate amount to cover a very much larger field of work. In other words, the vote as it stands to-day is equivalent to a very large increase when you consider the larger number of slaughtered animals it will cover by reason of the reduced indemnity.

My hon. friend from Brant (Mr. Good) states that we should go easy about handing out advice to farmers. I agree with him and accept that advice myself. I think I know enough about farming to be the last man to hand out advice too freely to a farmer, especially to one who has been

on a particular farm nearly all his life and knows better than any other man just what that farm can produce. At the same time, there are many other activities in connection with research work, without being too personal or hurting the susceptibilities of anyone by handing out too much advice. When I used to regard those sitting in the seats of the responsible, I took the same attitude, and I think I was justified. We do not mind taking advice from those who knorw at least as much as ourselves, but there has been a disposition, especially in connection with prairie agriculture, by people who do not know the prairies and cannot understand why we are wedded to grain farming, to advise us to engage in mixed farming. If they were on the prairies they would know how difficult it is to get away from grain farming and to gradually go into live stock. Many have tried it and have been driven out from one cause and another. But every time we gain a step in that direction we are making so much headway, and it will be found that our exports of dairy butter are increasing year by year in spite of setbacks.
I think I have covered all the points raised, Mr. Chairman.

tion which I think this party is entitled to. A year ago I moved for a return of all papers and correspondence in connection with it. This man has no other recourse. The matter has already been submitted to the new Government, and they do not see fit to give it any further consideration. The man is absolutely ruined by the loss which he has sustained, and he submits the evidence, but the evidence of the inspector is to be taken in preference to that of this man. It is a nice state of affairs if Parliament is going to delegate to the minister, and the minister delegates to somebody else, the authority in connection with this matter. We are a little too much inclined to throw the responsibility on somebody else, on the Civil Service Commission or something of that kind. Too much of that has been done already during the present session. That commission is responsible up to a certain point. After that the ministers are responsible. It was quite apparent to

624387,ca.proc.d.1922-04-20.1.10.113,1922-04-20,81e9d110-f6b1-4643-a4a5-d110dba9135f,ca.m.7827,Mr. MOTHERWELL:,Minister of Agriculture,QUESTIONS,PENITENTIARY ACT AMENDMENT,,I have to plead ignorance regarding the incident in connection with that hon. gentleman. I have to take him as I find him. I was very busy at the time that incident occurred, and I was not as close a reader of the newspapers as I am now, so that the incident escaped my attention. I was not reading many eastern newspapers at that time, and I do not think it appeared in the western newspapers.

As regards the bunch of hogs to which my hon. friend refers, an injustice may have been done. Sometimes justice falls short; we have known innocent men to be hanged, and we may expect a similar fatality to be meted out sometimes to a hog, to the detriment of the owner. All I say is that the evidence is against my hon. friend and his friend. That is, I think, what my predecessor claims, and he, last year, took the ground that, in the absence of contrary evidence, he had to stand by his officials. If, at the instance of every hon. member who chose to stand up loyally for his constituents, as he should do, we

threw down our inspectors, we would soon have no inspectors at all. I do not mean to say that, if the weight of evidence warrants our doing so, we should not dismiss an inspector and get another one and make proper restitution to the man who is wronged. Since, however, I have taken charge of this department, I have had an amazingly large number of these old, laid-on-the-shelf claims tried out on the new minister to see if he is easy enough to come across. I was not very long in this position until I had all kinds of representations how to do things and how to save the nation generally, amongst others, these old claims that had been threshed over, some of them repeatedly, in this House. While I admit that, in some cases, an injustice may have been done, I cannot find any injustice in this case, and with the absence of any weight of evidence to the contrary, I must stand by the decision of my officials and my predecessor. Nothing would give me more pleasure than to correct a wrong; and if this man had been unjustly dealt with, it would be a great pleasure to right the wrong, apart from the fact that that would be the ordinary work of my department. I have not, however, found that any injustice has been done. Another gentleman-I will not mention the name-wrote me the nicest letter comprising three or four pages, and it almost persuaded me that he had a case. I never received a finer letter, and I went to my deputy and the Veterinary Director General and I said: ""Here is a man who has been grievously wronged."" He was the worst humbug of the whole of them; but he nearly put it over me, and I felt I was badly fooled. You cannot go by appearances, nor by the skill with which people present their case, because sometimes the presentation is done rather decently and gentlemanly. My staff protected me on that occasion, and I did not come across because this man was the worst of the lot.
This is the contract that must be signed by all men who claim they are eligible to be recompensed for hogs slaughtered on account of cholera, and this was signed by Mr. Alderson:
In consideration of the granting of a license to me, I hereby agree:

column2: To maintain my hogs in a clean, sanitary condition.
To sell no hogs except for immediate slaughter.
To notify the veterinary inspector if sickness appears among my -hogs.

column1: Supply-Live Stock
The fourth is the crux of the whole matter.

column2: To forfeit all claim for compensation in case it is necessary to destroy any of my hogs as a result of hog cholera unless it can be shown that the infection came from some other source than from feeding garbage.

column1: In the absence of any proof that this hog cholera came from any other source, and in the fact of the presence of garbage uncooked being discovered in the troughs, what was I to do hut ask that this bargain be abided by? I sometimes wonder if we can get away from this proposition of cooking garbage. Those who do not believe in cooking garbage, who do so only under compulsion, who think it only a fake to have to cook garbage and that the Government is simply putting them to a lot of expense in buying a boiler and burning fuel, will, if you let them, cook the garbage in a slovenly manner. They will simply warm it up. This man may have simply warmed up the garbage because the disease germs were not killed. There was no evidence of the disease occurring in any other way, and, therefore, it must have come from the garbage. In the United States, the cooking of garbage is dispensed with. Hog cholera is so prevalent there that some sort of antitoxin is used, with which the animals are inoculated when young, the necessity of cooking garbage being thus avoided, as the antitoxin renders the hogs comparatively immune. Hog cholera is not sufficiently bad in this country to make it necessary for us to go to that expense. The next best thing is to take care of 90 per cent of the source of contagion which is known from actual experiment, to be from this uncooked garbage from hotels and such places. I hope the time will not come when we have to dispense with this matter of cooking garbage, because the whole country would be filled with cholera. I have looked carefully into the correspondence in this case, and I can read some of it; but in the absence of evidence to the contrary, there was nothing for me to do but to abide by the decision of my officials. As regards the charge against the Veterinary Director General that he is dishonest, I am not going to enter an action against my hon. friend. I have not found that to be the case at all. The Veterinary Director General may have his short-comings, as we all have, but I do not believe that dishonesty is one of them.

,Liberal,,William Richard Motherwell,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=81e9d110-f6b1-4643-a4a5-d110dba9135f&Language=E&Section=ALL
