imagine that, before expressing so decided an opinion, he would have taken the trouble to read the return through in full. If he had done so, he would have found that compensation was not withheld because the hogs were fed garbage. The officials departed from that contention, and they finally withheld compensation because the department had not been notified that cholera or sickness existed in the herd. The minister will find that there are affidavits furnished by the man who suffered the loss, by his son and by his general manager, that they were not aware of any sickness in the herd; and if so, it would be absolutely impossible for them to notify the department of sickness. More than that, I should like to ask: Is it reasonable to suppose that, with hogs that were valued in the neighbourhood of some $10,000, anyone who had been engaged in this business for many years would be so reckless as to take chances of having cholera develop in his herd? Who had a greater interest in maintaining the health of the herd, the owner or the inspectors of the department? The owner had everything at stake. He was anxious to continue in business and see that disease did not develop in his herd. He had one of the most up-to-date appliances for cooking the food that was to be found anywhere in the country, and if you look through the return you will find that he was finally notified that he could not receive compensation because he had not notified the department that disease existed in his herd. Why did not the inspector, when he notified his officials at Toronto, request them to inspect the premises that were complained of instead of giving the name of another person? And why did he withhold this from the first return brought down? It was not until he was ordered to bring it down in a further return that the information was tabled. Should the minister get up and attempt to ridicule anyone who stands for the rights of the people of this country? There is a court of appeal to which litigants may have resort, but in this case the Veterinary Director General appears to be the final judge, and the minister quietly accepts any statement he makes, so that the party who is aggrieved, it does not matter who he may be, has no further recourse. Is not that a strange condition of affairs in a country like this, when a citizen can have his rights brushed aside in that manner in the face of sworn evidence that substantiates his claim? All that the man asked for was a board of arbitrators who should go into the matter,
Supply-Live Stock

and if they decided against him he was prepared to accept their decision. But he did not wish to be shut out on the word of an inspector. What sort of tribunal is there in the Department of Agriculture, in connection with the Health of Animals branch, if people are to receive sudh treatment and there is no appeal from the decision of the Veterinary Director General? This is too serious a matter to be allowed to pass unheeded, because we are spending hundreds of thousands of dollars in this business.

I would ask the minister another question. Does he approve of spending $467,535 for the eradication of tubercular disease in pure bred herds, and only $98,000 in herds supplying milk to the people of the towns and cities? In connection with milk that is supplied to the municipalities only $98,000 is spent for the purpose of eradicating disease, although to-day so much attention is being paid to the children in the schools, who are being advised to drink more milk in order to build up their physique. In view of that fact, is it right or fair that the herds that supply the city people with milk should be discriminated against as has been done in the past? If the minister is anxious to preserve the health of the people, this item should be increased considerably. I am not finding fault with paying out this amount of money for the eradication of disease in pure bred herds, but I say that it is unfair that the herds supplying milk for home consumption should receive such a small amount for this purpose.

624459,ca.proc.d.1922-04-20.1.10.185,1922-04-20,81e9d110-f6b1-4643-a4a5-d110dba9135f,ca.m.7827,Mr. MOTHERWELL:,Minister of Agriculture,QUESTIONS,PENITENTIARY ACT AMENDMENT,,No, I do not think he would go down there for that purpose. While my civil government estimates were under discussion, I stated quite plainly the primary reason for Mr. Marshall's appointment, and I read the Order in Council to the House. I pointed out that we were having an investigation into the working of the Agricultural Instruction Act with a view to its possible continuance, discontinuance or amendment. Some phases of the act were under discussion when it was first launched, one of them being the basis of allocation, and I think that is a proper subject for reconsideration and further discussion. The present basis may be the best obtainable; but there is no harm in inquiring into the matter in order to see if there is a more equitable basis and also to find out first hand from the various provincial ministers of agriculture just what suggestions or amendments, if any, they would wish to make to the act. I am sorry to report that Mr. Marshall has been ill for the last three or four weeks and has not been able to continue his work. In the course of his work, he had a very bad attack of ""flu"" and has been in bed for nearly a month, so that we have not received that report yet. In view of the prospects of an early session next year, it may not be necessary to take action this session but we would like to have the act re-enacted this session with such amendments as may be found necessary, so that the provinces will know authoritatively that they can plan their work on the assumption that this work is going to be continued. I hope to be able to have the act re-enacted this session, and it may be found possible to incorporate some of the suggestions made by the hon. member for Saltcoats (Mr. Sales) with regard to removing the overlapping of provincial and Dominion activities. In this way some activities which are now carried on by the Dominion might be set apart for the provinces with Dominion oversight. These are all tentative propositions that could be decided upon only after careful examination into the work in the various provinces, and that work has already been begun.
As regards Mr. Marshall's trip to Florida, since that matter has been brought up so many times, I have no objection to

going into it. I do not know why any hon. gentleman should think that I was sending Mr. Marshall or anybody else to Florida for a joy ride or jaunt, for no particular purpose. I have been making inquiries into the matter, and find that the exhibition there has been running for a considerable number of years, I do not know how many.

It is, therefore, not an exhibition that has been suddenly organized by the Minister of the Interior for the purpose of permitting one of the staff to go on a joy ride or anything of that nature. I am not sure whether it was organized under the late government; it may have been tried out by my predecessor. In any event, I have a report from an officer in the Interior Department giving some of the results of Mr. Marshall's trip, stating that he addressed a large assemblage there of some 8,000 people and received a large quantity of front-page advertising by way of reports in many newspapers, advertising that would cost $15,000 or $20,000 at ordinarj advertising rates. Notwithstanding the doubt that was thrown on the likelihood of receiving any immigrants from that part of the world, I have a number of clippings intimating that many people at that exhibition were farmers, and already, as a direct result of that exhibition and of the address given by Mr. Marshall, some immigrants have arrived in Canada. Therefore, this trip was not entirely fruitless. Two other officials were there in charge ol the exhibits, and this was a regular annual event organized years ago and held in the same place as formerly for the same purpose of reaching possible immigrants, many of whom were at the exhibition. My information goes to indicate that, in the immediate neighbourhood, there are about 6.000 Canadians, many of whom, it is felt, would be desirous, if they knew the facts, t of returning to Canada, and I think this is a most fruitful ground for doing immigration work.

My desire to get some information with regard to this matter has been prompted by the evident disposition on the part of some people to see that the province of Ontario contributes its fair proportion of the expenditure of this country and yet is denied advantages which other provinces are receiving at the hands of the Government. The questions which I submitted to the minister with reference to the item which was allowed to stand over, were prompted by a desire to obtain this information, and the same is true with regard to experimental farms. The other night when I asked for information, we were simply told that Ontario was an old province and that we did not require anything of this kind. Now that we are discussing another vote we are told by the minister that Mr. Duncan Marshall has been employed trying to devise a better system by which larger grants will be given to some provinces than they are receiving at present.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Donald Sutherland,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=39733e89-5c63-44ea-a981-bc71336702b7&Language=E&Section=ALL
624461,ca.proc.d.1922-04-20.1.10.187,1922-04-20,81e9d110-f6b1-4643-a4a5-d110dba9135f,ca.m.7827,Mr. MOTHERWELL:,Minister of Agriculture,QUESTIONS,PENITENTIARY ACT AMENDMENT,,I never made the statement my hon. friend attributes to me. Surely he misunderstood me. As a matter of fact, the question of allocation came up when the act was first introduced, or at least the year after. The question as to whether the allocation should be based on straight population or on rural population is one of the debatable things that may come up, as it has come up before. It is not a new question, and personally I have no strong views upon it; but I take the ground that in some cases the grant might reasonably be smaller than in others. We have nine provinces. Suppose one province had no agriculture at all. That is an extreme view, but it is not an impossible one, because a province might be wholly engaged in manufacturing, mining, or lumbering. In such a case, should we be justified in making an allocation for agriculture where no agriculture existed? As I say, that is taking an extreme view; but just in proportion to the extent to which agriculture is pursued should the allocation be made. Whether a province is very largely engaged in agriculture, or is engaged in the industry only to a small extent, is a consideration that should surely have a bearing on the allocation when it is primarily for agriculture. That is a debatable question and it will be discussed when the matter is under consideration. However, it is not the subject for present investigation at all. The subject for discussion is the probable extension of agri-
culture, along the lines I have intimated, where we might avoid overlapping.

,Liberal,,William Richard Motherwell,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=81e9d110-f6b1-4643-a4a5-d110dba9135f&Language=E&Section=ALL
624462,ca.proc.d.1922-04-20.1.10.188,1922-04-20,39733e89-5c63-44ea-a981-bc71336702b7,ca.m.2365,Mr. SUTHERLAND:,,QUESTIONS,PENITENTIARY ACT AMENDMENT,,The minister

practically denied what I stated, but he concluded by arguing rather in support of the view I have formed of his position. I have been charging the department with a desire to discriminate against provinces on the basis of population, and now he says that a province that is largely engaged in manufacturing should not receive the same consideration as a province almost entirely engaged in agriculture. Well, I presume that, so far as his remarks in regard to manufacturing provinces is concerned, the province of Ontario stands out, if anything, a little in advance of any other province. I do not know whether Ontario is the one the minister has in mind, but you can easily realise where his argument would lead to. If you say that a province that will not derive any benefit from the grant shall not be required to contribute to the payment of it, that is a different matter. But if some provinces are asked to contribute practically one-half of the revenues of the country and are to be denied all the advantages that other provinces receive, then I say that this discrimination is going too far. And that is practically what we were told the other night by the minister with regard to experimental farms. He said that an old province like Ontario can derive no great benefit from these farms. I contend, on the contrary, that there are great benefits which we can get from a proper expenditure. I am not criticising the amount spent, but I should like to know whether we shall have an opportunity of further discussing this matter when Mr. Duncan Marshall's report is submitted to the House, as I presume it will be.
